bounded_slice.candidate: RFC 9053 algorithm identification as a candidate standard binding for digest/hash identity in an evidence envelope

primary_source.title: RFC 9053: CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE): Initial Algorithms
inspected_sections: 2.1 ECDSA including Table 1 and hash-substitution security consideration

bounded_slice.tested_scope: Static inspection of exactly one official RFC Editor primary source, RFC 9053. Tested only whether this source itself supplies an unambiguous standard identifier for an application-level content digest together with digest bytes that can be persisted inside the already-signed deterministic evidence payload/protected profile. No second public source, digest computation, encoder implementation, cryptographic execution, external service, protected-primary action, manual-user execution, scheduler mutation, or other-worker/downstream/O semantic input was consumed.
observations: RFC 9053 states that algorithm tables carry a wire value used for an algorithm, including use in the algorithm header parameter of a COSE message.

For ECDSA, RFC 9053 assigns signature algorithm identifiers such as ES256=-7, where the signature algorithm already fixes SHA-256; it also warns that changing the hash function can enable substitution attacks and says this is mitigated by including the signature algorithm identifier in the protected-header bucket.
RFC 9053 separately notes for EdDSA that an application may define message content to be a hash value and transport the COSE object containing that hash value separately from the original content.

However, the inspected RFC does not define a standalone application-level content-digest algorithm identifier paired with arbitrary digest bytes. Its concrete wire identifiers are COSE algorithm identifiers for signature/MAC/KDF/etc. algorithms, not a generic digest-method field for evidence payload content.
bounded_slice.inference: Negative/insufficient result for this exact child: RFC 9053 is strong evidence that cryptographic algorithm identity must be bound into protected/signed material to avoid algorithm substitution, but this source alone does not standardize an independent content-digest identifier plus digest bytes for an evidence envelope. Therefore a profile cannot claim unambiguous standalone digest identification merely by storing digest bytes or by reusing a COSE signature-algorithm identifier when the content digest is conceptually separate. The evidence schema must either define its own fixed digest algorithm or adopt a separate standard digest-identifier registry/specification in a later bounded slice.
bounded_slice.uncertainty: No claim is made about every COSE extension or registry outside RFC 9053, because no second source was inspected. No implementation test established that scheduled Chat can compute, encode, sign, or verify the digest/package. This result is limited to what RFC 9053 itself specifies.
bounded_slice.replayability: digest bytes can be carried as signed payload data in principle, but replayable interpretation of an independent digest requires an unambiguous digest-method identifier not supplied by this inspected source
bounded_slice.hidden_executor_absence: static specification inspection required no external execution handoff; concrete hashing/encoding/signing/verification capabilities remain unresolved children and are not assumed
